Other than taking the parameter methods in app.route, there isn’t much to this application. We’re showing a tag for an embedded video, which for us to render only involves returning a string of the tag.

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
text:
In a previous post I used ellipses to put hard bounds on where a moose could have been between two GPS fixes, assuming only a maximum possible speed. That approach answers “where could it not have been” and never says anything about likelihood. This post is about the complementary probabilistic tool, and about the single most widely used stochastic model of animal movement: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process.
The OU process is a diffusion with a linear restoring force. Interpreted for moose, it says that the animal is pulled back towards a home-range centre and buffeted by random motion, and it is the special case of the general Fokker-Planck framework in which the density stays Gaussian and every quantity of interest is available in closed form. That tractability is exactly why it is a natural first model, and also why it is too restrictive to be the last one. In the next post I lift the restrictions one at a time and build a general Fokker-Planck model of moose movement; this post establishes the baseline that the general model has to beat.

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
text:
From paths to densities
Start with the individual. An It^o stochastic differential equation (SDE) says that a small change in position over a small change in time has a predictable part and a random part:
\[dX_t = \mu(X_t, t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t, t)\,dW_t,\]
where \(\mu\) is the drift vector, \(\sigma\) the diffusion matrix, and \(W_t\) a Wiener process (Brownian motion). Each sample path of this SDE is a plausible trajectory for one animal: drift is the average or directed motion, diffusion is the unpredictable jitter.
The density \(p(x, t)\) of where the animal is likely to be then obeys the Fokker-Planck equation (also called the Kolmogorov forward equation):
\[\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot \bigl(\mu\, p\bigr) + \frac{1}{2}\,\partial_i \partial_j \bigl(D_{ij}\, p\bigr), \qquad D = \sigma\sigma^{\top}.\]
The SDE and the Fokker-Planck equation are two descriptions of the same stochastic process: the SDE is the language of paths, the PDE the language of densities. The OU process is what you get when the drift is linear and the diffusion is constant and isotropic.

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
text:
The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model
Moose are not diffusing gas molecules, but they do have a strong tendency to stay within a home range. The OU model encodes that with a drift that pulls the animal back towards a centre \(c\),
\[\mu(x) = -\kappa\,(x - c),\]
so that far from the centre the drift is large and inward, and near the centre it is negligible. The two parameters have clear interpretations:

\(\kappa > 0\) is the fidelity to the home range, in units of \(1/\text{time}\). Its reciprocal \(1/\kappa\) is the characteristic time over which the animal forgets its current position and relaxes back towards the centre. It is the relaxation or memory time.
\(\sigma\) is the restlessness, in units of \(\text{distance}/\sqrt{\text{time}}\). It is not a speed: it is the strength of the random component, and its units are those of a diffusion coefficient’s square root.

Because the drift is linear and the noise is constant, the model is exactly solvable. The stationary distribution of positions is Gaussian,
\[p_\infty(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi s^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-c)^2}{2s^2}\right), \qquad s^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa},\]
so the home-range size \(s\) is set by the ratio of restlessness to fidelity. In two dimensions the same model gives an isotropic Gaussian around \(c\) with per-axis standard deviation \(s\), so the radius from the centre follows a Rayleigh distribution with mean \(s\sqrt{\pi/2}\). The full time-dependent solution is also known exactly: starting from a point at the centre, the position at time \(t\) is Gaussian with mean \(c\) and variance
\[s^2(t) = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\left(1 - e^{-2\kappa t}\right),\]
which approaches \(s^2\) at rate \(\kappa\). This is the property that makes the OU model the reference point: from two numbers, \(\kappa\) and \(\sigma\), and a centre, you can write down the entire distribution at any time.

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
section: The density equation for the OU model
text:
The density equation for the OU model
To get the density equation itself onto the page, the Python script below solves the one-dimensional Fokker-Planck equation for the OU model on a grid with an explicit finite-volume scheme. The probability current is
\[J = -\kappa\,(x - c)\,p - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\frac{\partial p}{\partial x},\]
and it is discretized in flux form with the advective part upwinded and the diffusive part centred. The flux is set to zero at the walls, so total probability is conserved exactly, and the initial condition is a point mass at the centre. The script then compares three things: the simulated moose from the Rust program, the numerical PDE solution, and the analytic Gaussian.
"""Fokker-Planck and analytic solutions of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck moose model.

The companion Rust crate ``moose_ou`` simulates virtual moose whose positions
follow an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, that is, the It^o SDE

    dx = -kappa (x - c) dt + sigma dW

The density of those positions, p(x, t), obeys the Fokker-Planck equation

    dp/dt = kappa d/dx[(x - c) p] + (sigma^2 / 2) d^2p/dx^2.

This module solves that PDE directly on a grid with an explicit finite-volume
scheme (upwinded drift, centred diffusion, no-flux walls), and plots the PDE
solution against the simulated moose and against the analytic OU transition
density,

    X_t ~ Normal(c, (sigma^2 / 2 kappa) (1 - exp(-2 kappa t))).

Run the Rust crate first so that ``data/moose_positions.csv`` and
``data/moose_track.csv`` exist.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

KAPPA = 0.5
"""Home-range fidelity, in 1/h."""

SIGMA = 1.0
"""Exploratory jitter, in km/sqrt(h)."""

T_END = 20.0
"""Simulation length, in h."""

CENTRE = 0.0
"""Home-range centre, in km."""


def load_positions(path: str | Path) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Load the final ``(x, y)`` positions of every moose from ``path``."""
    data = np.loadtxt(path, delimiter=",", skiprows=1)
    return data[:, 0], data[:, 1]


def load_track(path: str | Path) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Load a representative ``(t, x, y)`` trajectory from ``path``."""
    data = np.loadtxt(path, delimiter=",", skiprows=1)
    return data[:, 0], data[:, 1], data[:, 2]


def analytic_variance(t: float, *, kappa: float = KAPPA, sigma: float = SIGMA) -> float:
    """Variance of the OU process started at the centre.

    The variance relaxes from zero towards ``sigma**2 / (2 kappa)`` like
    ``1 - exp(-2 kappa t)``.
    """
    return sigma**2 / (2 * kappa) * (1 - np.exp(-2 * kappa * t))


def stationary_sd(*, kappa: float = KAPPA, sigma: float = SIGMA) -> float:
    """Stationary standard deviation per axis, ``sigma / sqrt(2 kappa)``."""
    return sigma / math.sqrt(2 * kappa)


def analytic_pdf(
    x: np.ndarray,
    t: float,
    *,
    kappa: float = KAPPA,
    sigma: float = SIGMA,
    centre: float = CENTRE,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Transition density of the OU process at time ``t``."""
    variance = analytic_variance(t, kappa=kappa, sigma=sigma)
    return np.exp(-0.5 * (x - centre) ** 2 / variance) / math.sqrt(
        2 * math.pi * variance
    )


def solve_fokker_planck(
    extent: float = 5.0,
    dx: float = 0.01,
    dt: float = 5e-5,
    *,
    kappa: float = KAPPA,
    sigma: float = SIGMA,
    t_end: float = T_END,
    centre: float = CENTRE,
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Finite-volume solution of the 1D Fokker-Planck equation.

    The probability current is written in flux form,

        J = -kappa (x - c) p - (sigma^2 / 2) dp/dx,

    with the advective part upwinded and the diffusive part centred, and the
    time step is explicit. The flux is set to zero at the two walls, so mass
    is conserved exactly. Upwinding adds a small numerical diffusion of size
    ``|v| dx / 2``, which is the main discretization error.

    Returns ``(x, times, snapshots, masses, means, variances)``.
    """
    x = np.arange(-extent, extent + dx / 2, dx)
    n_steps = round(t_end / dt)
    record_every = max(1, n_steps // 400)

    p = np.zeros_like(x)
    p[np.argmin(np.abs(x - centre))] = 1.0 / dx  # Start as a point mass

    diffusivity = sigma**2 / 2

    def step(density: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        # Probability current at the interior cell faces.
        velocity_face = -kappa * (0.5 * (x[:-1] + x[1:]) - centre)
        upwind = np.where(velocity_face > 0, density[:-1], density[1:])
        advective = velocity_face * upwind
        diffusive = -diffusivity * (density[1:] - density[:-1]) / dx

        # No-flux walls, so the interior update telescopes to zero.
        current = np.concatenate(([0.0], advective + diffusive, [0.0]))
        return density - dt / dx * (current[1:] - current[:-1])

    times = [0.0]
    snapshots = [p.copy()]
    masses = [float(np.sum(p) * dx)]
    means = [float(np.sum(x * p) * dx)]
    variances = [float(np.sum((x - centre) ** 2 * p) * dx)]

    for step_index in range(n_steps):
        p = step(p)

        if (step_index + 1) % record_every == 0:
            times.append((step_index + 1) * dt)
            snapshots.append(p.copy())
            masses.append(float(np.sum(p) * dx))
            means.append(float(np.sum(x * p) * dx))
            variances.append(float(np.sum((x - centre) ** 2 * p) * dx))

    return (
        x,
        np.array(times),
        np.array(snapshots),
        np.array(masses),
        np.array(means),
        np.array(variances),
    )


def diagnostics(
    masses: np.ndarray,
    means: np.ndarray,
    variances: np.ndarray,
    *,
    kappa: float = KAPPA,
    sigma: float = SIGMA,
    t_end: float = T_END,
    centre: float = CENTRE,
) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Compare the PDE solution at ``t_end`` with the analytic values."""
    return {
        "mass": float(masses[-1]),
        "pde_variance": float(variances[-1]),
        "analytic_variance": float(analytic_variance(t_end, kappa=kappa, sigma=sigma)),
        "pde_mean": float(means[-1]),
        "analytic_mean": float(centre),
    }


def print_diagnostics(diag: dict[str, float]) -> None:
    """Print the PDE-versus-analytic comparison quoted in the blog post."""
    print("Fokker-Planck PDE versus analytic solution:")
    print(f"  {'mass at T:':<20}{diag['mass']:.6f} (should be 1.000000)")
    print(f"  {'PDE variance at T:':<20}{diag['pde_variance']:.6f}")
    print(f"  {'analytic variance:':<20}{diag['analytic_variance']:.6f}")
    print(f"  {'PDE mean at T:':<20}{diag['pde_mean']:.6f}")
    print(f"  {'analytic mean:':<20}{diag['analytic_mean']:.6f}")


def plot_comparison(
    x_positions: np.ndarray,
    y_positions: np.ndarray,
    t_track: np.ndarray,
    x_track: np.ndarray,
    y_track: np.ndarray,
    solve: tuple[
        np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray
    ],
    output: str | Path,
    *,
    kappa: float = KAPPA,
    sigma: float = SIGMA,
    t_end: float = T_END,
    centre: float = CENTRE,
) -> Path:
    """Render the four-panel comparison figure and return the written path."""
    x, times, snapshots, _masses, _means, variances = solve

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 10))

    # (a) One simulated moose trajectory.
    ax = axes[0, 0]
    points = ax.scatter(x_track, y_track, c=t_track, cmap="viridis", s=6)
    ax.scatter([centre], [centre], marker="+", color="black", s=150, linewidths=2)
    ax.annotate(
        "home-range\ncentre",
        (centre, centre),
        xytext=(10, -25),
        textcoords="offset points",
        fontsize=9,
    )
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
    ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("y (km)")
    ax.set_title("One simulated moose, coloured by time (h)")
    fig.colorbar(points, ax=ax, label="t (h)")

    # (b) Final positions of all virtual moose against the analytic density.
    ax = axes[0, 1]
    ax.scatter(x_positions, y_positions, s=3, alpha=0.25, color="steelblue")
    radius = np.linspace(0, 2 * math.pi, 200)
    sd = stationary_sd(kappa=kappa, sigma=sigma)
    for level in (1, 2):
        ax.plot(
            level * sd * np.cos(radius),
            level * sd * np.sin(radius),
            color="darkred",
            linewidth=2,
        )
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
    ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("y (km)")
    ax.set_title("Final positions with 1 and 2 sd analytic contours")
    ax.set_xlim(-4, 4)
    ax.set_ylim(-4, 4)

    # (c) 1D marginal: particles, Fokker-Planck PDE, and the analytic density.
    ax = axes[1, 0]
    bins = np.linspace(-4, 4, 41)
    ax.hist(
        x_positions,
        bins=bins,
        density=True,
        color="steelblue",
        alpha=0.6,
        label="simulated moose",
    )
    x_fine = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
    ax.plot(
        x_fine,
        analytic_pdf(x_fine, t_end, kappa=kappa, sigma=sigma, centre=centre),
        color="black",
        linewidth=2,
        label="analytic density at t = T",
    )
    ax.plot(
        x,
        snapshots[-1],
        color="darkred",
        linestyle="--",
        linewidth=2,
        label="Fokker-Planck PDE",
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("density (1/km)")
    ax.set_title(f"Marginal distribution at t = {t_end:.0f} h")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    # (d) Relaxation of the variance towards its equilibrium value.
    ax = axes[1, 1]
    ax.plot(
        times,
        variances,
        color="darkred",
        linestyle="--",
        label="Fokker-Planck PDE",
    )
    t_fine = np.linspace(0, t_end, 300)
    ax.plot(
        t_fine,
        analytic_variance(t_fine, kappa=kappa, sigma=sigma),
        color="black",
        linewidth=2,
        label="analytic",
    )
    ax.axhline(sigma**2 / (2 * kappa), color="grey", linewidth=1, label="equilibrium")
    ax.set_xlabel("t (h)")
    ax.set_ylabel("variance (km$^2$)")
    ax.set_title("Relaxation of the density to equilibrium")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    fig.suptitle(
        "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck moose movement: particles versus the Fokker-Planck equation",
    )
    fig.tight_layout()

    output_path = Path(output)
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(output_path, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
    plt.close(fig)
    return output_path


def run(
    positions_path: str | Path = "data/moose_positions.csv",
    track_path: str | Path = "data/moose_track.csv",
    output: str | Path = "figures/moose_fokker_planck.png",
) -> Path:
    """Solve, compare, plot, and print diagnostics for the OU moose model."""
    x_positions, y_positions = load_positions(positions_path)
    t_track, x_track, y_track = load_track(track_path)

    solve = solve_fokker_planck()
    _x, _times, _snapshots, masses, means, variances = solve

    output_path = plot_comparison(
        x_positions, y_positions, t_track, x_track, y_track, solve, output
    )

    print_diagnostics(diagnostics(masses, means, variances))
    print(f"\nSaved plot to: {output_path}")
    return output_path


def main() -> None:
    """Console-script entry point."""
    run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()



Particles, the Fokker-Planck equation, and the analytic density agreeing for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck moose model


The three routes to the answer agree. The printed diagnostics are:
Fokker-Planck PDE versus analytic solution:
  mass at T:          1.000000 (should be 1.000000)
  PDE variance at T:  1.007964
  analytic variance:  1.000000
  PDE mean at T:      -0.000000
  analytic mean:      0.000000
The mass is conserved to machine precision, as it must be for a no-flux boundary. The variance is high by about \(0.8\%\), and the reason is instructive: first-order upwinding of the drift term adds an artificial diffusion of size roughly \(|v|\,\Delta x/2\). Halving the grid spacing roughly halves that bias. This is a reminder that “solving the Fokker-Planck equation numerically” always means solving a discretization of it, and the discretization has its own physics.

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
text:
Properties of the OU model
The OU model’s special structure is what makes it both useful and, in the end, restrictive.

Exact solvability. Linear drift and constant diffusion keep the density Gaussian forever. The stationary and transition densities are normal, so predictions are closed-form.
A Gaussian home range. The stationary distribution is a single isotropic bell centred on \(c\) with standard deviation \(s = \sigma/\sqrt{2\kappa}\). Its area is a home-range size, and its contours are a utilization distribution. It has no notion of shape beyond a circle.
Exponential relaxation with a spectral gap. The Fokker-Planck operator for the OU model has Gaussian eigenfunctions with eigenvalues \(-n\kappa\), so every deviation from equilibrium decays at a known exponential rate and the slowest mode is \(1/\kappa\). Equilibrium is approached, and how fast is computable.
Closed moment equations. The mean relaxes to \(c\) like \(e^{-\kappa t}\) and the variance approaches \(s^2\) like \(e^{-2\kappa t}\), so the first two moments can be tracked without solving the PDE at all.
Reversibility. The OU process is in detailed balance: in equilibrium, every microscopic transition is balanced by its reverse, and there is no net circulation of probability. This is a strong restriction, and general models lose it.
Positivity and conservation. As for any Fokker-Planck model, \(p \ge 0\) is preserved and total probability is conserved with no-flux boundaries. Adding a sink term turns it into a model of mortality or of animals leaving the study area.
Infinite propagation speed. For \(\sigma > 0\) the equation is parabolic, so a point mass immediately has nonzero density everywhere. The moose could be anywhere, with minuscule but positive probability immediately, no matter how fast it would have to travel. This is in direct tension with the hard maximum-speed bound of the ellipse method.
A diffusion limit. Without drift the model is Brownian motion and the variance grows linearly, \(2Dt\). The OU process is the mean-reverting version of that random walk, which is why it sits underneath both random-walk models and macroscopic diffusion models.

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
text:
Strengths of the OU model

Interpretable parameters. Fidelity and restlessness are statements about the animal, not statistical conveniences, and they carry units a field biologist can reason about.
Closed-form answers for useful quantities. Home-range size, the time to settle, the overlap of two home ranges, and the expected time to encounter a fixed feature are all available without simulation.
A utilization distribution for free. The stationary density is what home-range and habitat analyses actually want, produced from two individual-level parameters.
It fits data. Because the transition density is Gaussian, the OU model is a linear Gaussian state-space model: it can be fitted to irregularly-spaced collar fixes by maximum likelihood or Kalman filtering, with measurement error handled explicitly (Hooten et al. 2017).
It is the right null model. In movement ecology the mean-reverting diffusion is the baseline against which more elaborate models are compared, much as Brownian motion is the baseline in phylogenetics.
It is a bridge. The OU process links individual movement rules to redistribution patterns through the continuum limit in the movement ecology literature (Turchin 1998; Nathan et al. 2008).

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
text:
Defects of the OU model
Every strength above is also a defect when the animal does not cooperate, and moose mostly do not.

The home range is a single Gaussian blob. Real ranges are often multi-modal, elongated along valleys and ridges, and asymmetrical. An isotropic OU process cannot represent any shape.
The drift is linear. There is no habitat in the model. Food, cover, and terrain should bend the drift, not a spring to a point.
The diffusion is constant and isotropic. Movement is equally easy in all directions and everywhere, which is false across snow, muskeg, forest, and open ground, and false along corridors.
There are no boundaries. Rivers, lakes, highways, fences, and cliff lines are invisible to the model, even though they dominate where a moose can go.
There are no interactions. The model describes one animal in a fixed environment. It cannot represent avoidance of conspecifics, a cow and calf staying together, or predator risk.
There is no memory or behaviour. The process is Markovian with white noise and Gaussian steps. Real moose have behavioural states, autocorrelated moves, and heavy-tailed excursions that a single \(\sigma\) cannot produce.
The parameters are constant. Real fidelity and restlessness vary with season, snow, rut, and time of day. A stationary model over months is an average that may describe no moose in particular.
Only one animal at a time. Turning the density into a population model requires either independent copies (ignoring interaction) or coupling.
It grants infinite speed, as noted above, so it is not a physical bound and can assign probability to impossible jumps.

The next post repairs these one at a time by writing the Fokker-Planck equation in its general form: a habitat potential instead of a spring, a spatial diffusion field instead of a constant, barriers as boundary conditions, interactions as nonlocal couplings, behaviour as multiple states, and jumps as fractional diffusion.

title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model of Moose Movement
text:
Conclusion
The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is the natural first model of a moose with a home range: two interpretable parameters, an exact Gaussian answer, a known relaxation rate, and a clean path to fitting collar data. It is also a caricature. The rest of this series generalizes the density equation until the model can carry habitat, barriers, interactions, behaviour, and jumps, using the OU model as the baseline whose defects define the agenda.

title: A General Fokker-Planck Model of Moose Movement
text: In the previous post I built the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model of a moose with a home range, and ended with a list of nine defects and a promise: rebuild the model in the general Fokker-Planck form, repairing the defects one term at a time. That is this post. The OU model was the special case in which the drift is a spring, the diffusion is a constant, and everything stays Gaussian and closed-form. The general equation is the framework in which habitat, barriers, interactions, behavioural states, and jumps can all be written down explicitly. The price is that almost nothing in it is solvable by hand: every result below is computed numerically.

title: A General Fokker-Planck Model of Moose Movement
text:
The general equation
The Fokker-Planck equation for the density \(p(x,t)\) of an animal’s position, in the form that can carry all of the repairs at once, is
\[\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot \bigl(b[x,p]\, p\bigr) + \frac{1}{2}\,\partial_i \partial_j \bigl(D_{ij}(x)\, p\bigr) - \lambda(x)\,p.\]
Compared to the equation in the previous post, three things have become general. The drift \(b\) may depend on space through a habitat field and on the density itself through a nonlocal coupling. The diffusion \(D_{ij}\) is a field rather than a constant, so movement can be easier in some terrain than others. The sink term \(\lambda\) removes mass, modelling mortality or animals leaving the study area. Each change answers a specific defect from the OU list:

Habitat instead of a spring (defects 1 and 2). Write the drift as \(b = -\nabla U\) for a habitat potential \(U\), large where habitat is poor. The potential-function approach to movement is standard in ecology (Preisler et al. 2013); nothing forces \(U\) to be quadratic or its level sets to be circles, so the home range can be multi-modal and shaped like the landscape.
A diffusion field (defect 3). \(D(x)\) varies across snow, muskeg, forest, and open ground, and along corridors.
Barriers as boundary conditions (defect 4). Rivers, lakes, and highways become walls on which the probability current is set to zero, with gaps where crossing is possible.
Interactions as nonlocal coupling (defect 5). Each animal climbs the local density of conspecifics, \(b[x,p] = -\nabla U + \chi \, \nabla \log (G * p)\), where \(G\) is a smoothing kernel and \(\chi\) the attraction strength. This is a mean-field stand-in for the local attraction and alignment rules that organize real groups (Couzin et al. 2002).
Behaviour as multiple states (defects 6 and 7). Run several densities \(p_i\) at once, each with its own potential and diffusivity, coupled by switching rates \(q_{ij}\). A moose alternates between a tight core range and a wider exploratory mode; the observable density is the mixture.
Jumps as fractional diffusion (defect 9). Replace the Laplacian by the fractional Laplacian of order \(2\alpha\), so the diffusion term becomes \(D\,(-\Delta)^{\alpha} p\) with \(\alpha = 1\) the Brownian case and \(\alpha < 1\) a process that makes occasional long relocations (Metzler et al. 1994; Xie et al. 2015).

One property of the OU model survives generalization and becomes the workhorse check for everything below. With a constant scalar \(D\) and no-flux walls, the current \(J = -\nabla U\, p - D \nabla p\) vanishes identically for the Boltzmann equilibrium
\[p_\infty(x) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{U(x)}{D}\right),\]
which reduces to exactly the Gaussian of the previous post when \(U\) is the spring \(\kappa(x-c)^2/2\) and \(D = \sigma^2/2\). For constant \(D\), habitat alone determines where the animal concentrates; the numerical question is whether the scheme reproduces it.

title: A General Fokker-Planck Model of Moose Movement
section: Experiment 1: habitat, a river, and a bridge
text:
Experiment 1: habitat, a river, and a bridge
The Python script below puts the general equation on a two-dimensional landscape: a \(4 \times 4\) km domain on an \(81 \times 81\) grid with two Gaussian habitat wells (two home ranges), a river along \(x = 2\) km with a single bridge near \(y = 0.7\) km, and constant \(D = 0.5\ \text{km}^2/\text{h}\). All density starts in the left well. Three experiments are run: relaxation to equilibrium with and without the river, and a final run in which \(D(x)\) has a hot spot of easier movement near the right well, where the Boltzmann formula no longer applies.
"""A general Fokker-Planck model of moose movement in two dimensions.

This solves the Fokker-Planck equation

    dp/dt = -div[ b(x) p ] + d_i d_j [ D_ij(x) p ],

with a habitat potential U so that the drift is b = -grad U (plus an optional
nonlocal interaction term), a spatially varying diffusion D(x), and no-flux
walls around the domain and around a barrier (a river with a crossing).

Three experiments are reported:

1. equilibrium for a constant diffusion: p ~ exp(-U / D), including the effect
   of the barrier on how fast that equilibrium is approached;
2. the transient mixing of the two home-range lobes with and without the
   barrier;
3. a spatially varying diffusion, for which exp(-U / D) is no longer the
   stationary solution.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from moose_fp.numerics import total_variation

LENGTH = 4.0  # Domain side length, km
GRID = 81  # Cells per side
D0 = 0.5  # Base diffusion, km^2/h
DEPTH = 2.0  # Habitat well depth
WIDTH = 0.5  # Habitat well width, km


def build_domain(
    length: float = LENGTH,
    grid: int = GRID,
    depth: float = DEPTH,
    well_width: float = WIDTH,
):
    """Return ``(x, y, xx, yy, potential, solid)`` for the toy landscape.

    The landscape has two Gaussian habitat wells and a river at ``x = 2`` km
    with a single bridge near ``y = 0.7`` km. ``solid`` marks the cells that
    are walled off (the river outside the bridge).
    """
    x = np.linspace(0.0, length, grid)
    y = np.linspace(0.0, length, grid)
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing="ij")

    # Two home-range wells, one on each side of the river.
    wells = [(1.0, 2.0), (3.0, 2.0)]
    potential = np.zeros_like(xx)
    for wx, wy in wells:
        potential -= depth * np.exp(
            -((xx - wx) ** 2 + (yy - wy) ** 2) / (2 * well_width**2)
        )

    # A river at x = 2 with a single bridge at y ~ 0.7.
    solid = np.zeros_like(xx, dtype=bool)
    wall = np.isclose(xx, 2.0, atol=0.75 * (x[1] - x[0]))
    bridge = np.abs(yy - 0.7) < 0.2
    solid[wall & ~bridge] = True

    return x, y, xx, yy, potential, solid


def steady_state(potential, solid, diffusion, weights=None):
    """Boltzmann prediction p ~ exp(-U / D) on the open cells."""
    if weights is None:
        weights = np.ones_like(potential)
    p = np.where(solid, 0.0, weights * np.exp(-potential / diffusion))
    p /= p.sum()
    return p


def gradient(field, spacing):
    """Central gradient with second-order edges."""
    return np.gradient(field, spacing, edge_order=2)


def solve(
    potential,
    solid,
    diffusion,
    p0,
    t_end,
    interaction=0.0,
    record_times=(),
):
    """Explicit finite-volume integration of the general Fokker-Planck equation.

    ``diffusion`` may be a scalar or a two-dimensional array. ``interaction``
    is the strength of a nonlocal attraction towards the mean of the
    distribution (McKean-Vlasov term); zero means no interaction.

    Returns ``(p, dt, saved, open_)`` where ``saved`` maps each requested
    record time to a copy of the density at that time.
    """
    nx, ny = potential.shape
    dx = LENGTH / (nx - 1)
    dy = LENGTH / (ny - 1)

    if np.isscalar(diffusion):
        diffusion = np.full_like(potential, diffusion)

    bx, by = gradient(-potential, dx)

    d_max = float(np.max(diffusion[~solid]))
    b_max = max(float(np.max(np.abs(bx[~solid]))), float(np.max(np.abs(by[~solid]))))
    # 2D explicit stability: diffusion number D dt / dx^2 <= 1/4 and
    # advective CFL |b| dt / dx <= 1, with a safety factor.
    dt = 0.2 * min(dx**2 / d_max, dx / max(b_max, 1e-12))
    n_steps = round(t_end / dt)

    p = np.zeros_like(potential)
    p[:] = p0
    p[solid] = 0.0

    open_ = ~solid
    saved = {}
    next_record = 0

    for step in range(n_steps):
        drift_x, drift_y = bx, by
        if interaction != 0.0:
            smoothed = smooth(p)
            gx, gy = gradient(smoothed, dx)
            drift_x = bx - interaction * gx
            drift_y = by - interaction * gy

        flux_x = face_flux(p, drift_x, diffusion, solid, axis=0, spacing=dx)
        flux_y = face_flux(p, drift_y, diffusion, solid, axis=1, spacing=dy)

        divergence = divergence_from_flux(flux_x, flux_y, spacing=dx)
        p = p - dt * divergence
        p[solid] = 0.0
        p[p < 0.0] = 0.0

        if next_record < len(record_times) and (step + 1) * dt >= record_times[next_record]:
            saved[record_times[next_record]] = p.copy()
            next_record += 1

    return p, dt, saved, open_


def face_flux(p, drift, diffusion, solid, axis, spacing):
    """Advective (upwinded) plus diffusive flux on the cell faces."""
    if axis == 0:
        solid_face = solid[:-1, :] | solid[1:, :]
        drift_face = 0.5 * (drift[:-1, :] + drift[1:, :])
        diff_face = 0.5 * (diffusion[:-1, :] + diffusion[1:, :])
        left, right = p[:-1, :], p[1:, :]
    else:
        solid_face = solid[:, :-1] | solid[:, 1:]
        drift_face = 0.5 * (drift[:, :-1] + drift[:, 1:])
        diff_face = 0.5 * (diffusion[:, :-1] + diffusion[:, 1:])
        left, right = p[:, :-1], p[:, 1:]

    upwind = np.where(drift_face > 0, left, right)
    flux = drift_face * upwind - diff_face * (right - left) / spacing
    return np.where(solid_face, 0.0, flux)


def divergence_from_flux(flux_x, flux_y, spacing):
    """Divergence of a face-centred flux on a cell-centred grid."""
    nx, ny = flux_x.shape[0] + 1, flux_x.shape[1]
    divergence = np.zeros((nx, ny))

    face_x = np.zeros((nx + 1, ny))
    face_x[1:-1] = flux_x
    divergence += (face_x[1:] - face_x[:-1]) / spacing

    face_y = np.zeros((nx, ny + 1))
    face_y[:, 1:-1] = flux_y
    divergence += (face_y[:, 1:] - face_y[:, :-1]) / spacing

    return divergence


def smooth(field):
    """Small Gaussian smoothing used for the nonlocal interaction term."""
    from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter

    return gaussian_filter(field, sigma=2.0, mode="nearest")


def centre_delta(x, y, cx, cy, solid):
    """A point mass at the grid node nearest ``(cx, cy)``, normalised."""
    p = np.zeros((len(x), len(y)))
    i = int(np.argmin(np.abs(x - cx)))
    j = int(np.argmin(np.abs(y - cy)))
    p[i, j] = 1.0
    p[solid] = 0.0
    return p / p.sum()


def _plot(xx, yy, potential, solid, equilibrium, record_times, error_barrier,
          error_free, open_cells, p_variable, diffusion_field):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10.5))
    extent = [0, LENGTH, 0, LENGTH]

    ax = axes[0, 0]
    image = ax.imshow(potential.T, origin="lower", extent=extent, cmap="terrain")
    ax.contour(xx.T, yy.T, potential.T, levels=8, colors="black", linewidths=0.4)
    ax.imshow(
        np.where(solid, 1.0, np.nan).T,
        origin="lower",
        extent=extent,
        cmap="Greys",
        vmin=0,
        vmax=1,
        alpha=0.9,
    )
    ax.set_title("Habitat potential U (dark = good) and river with bridge")
    ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("y (km)")
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="U")

    ax = axes[0, 1]
    image = ax.imshow(equilibrium.T, origin="lower", extent=extent, cmap="viridis")
    ax.set_title(r"Equilibrium for constant $D$: $p \propto e^{-U/D}$")
    ax.set_xlabel("x (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("y (km)")
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="density")

    ax = axes[1, 0]
    ax.plot(record_times, error_barrier, color="darkred", linewidth=2, label="with river")
    ax.plot(record_times, error_free, color="steelblue", linewidth=2, label="no river")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel("t (h)")
    ax.set_ylabel("total-variation distance to equilibrium")
    ax.set_title("The river slows mixing but not the equilibrium")
    ax.legend()

    ax = axes[1, 1]
    scatter = ax.scatter(
        -potential[open_cells] / D0,
        np.log(p_variable[open_cells]),
        c=np.log10(diffusion_field[open_cells]),
        s=12,
        cmap="plasma",
    )
    fit = np.polyfit(-potential[open_cells] / D0, np.log(p_variable[open_cells]), 1)
    xs = np.linspace(
        (-potential[open_cells] / D0).min(), (-potential[open_cells] / D0).max(), 10
    )
    ax.plot(xs, np.polyval(fit, xs), color="black", linewidth=2, label=f"slope {fit[0]:.2f}")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$-U/D_0$")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\log p$ (steady state)")
    ax.set_title("Variable diffusion breaks the Boltzmann law")
    ax.legend()
    fig.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax, label=r"$\log_{10} D$")

    fig.suptitle("General Fokker-Planck model of moose movement")
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig


def run(output: str | Path = "figures/general_fp_2d.png") -> Path:
    """Run the three experiments, print diagnostics, and write the figure."""
    x, y, xx, yy, potential, solid = build_domain()

    equilibrium = steady_state(potential, solid, D0)

    # --- Experiment 1 and 2: barrier versus no barrier -------------------
    record_times = np.linspace(0.0, 60.0, 121)
    start = centre_delta(x, y, 1.0, 2.0, solid)

    _p_barrier, _dt, saved_barrier, _ = solve(
        potential, solid, D0, start, 60.0, record_times=tuple(record_times)
    )
    p_free, _, saved_free, _ = solve(
        potential, np.zeros_like(solid), D0, start, 60.0, record_times=tuple(record_times)
    )

    error_barrier = np.array(
        [total_variation(saved_barrier[t], equilibrium) for t in record_times]
    )
    error_free = np.array([total_variation(saved_free[t], equilibrium) for t in record_times])

    # --- Experiment 3: spatially varying diffusion -----------------------
    diffusion_field = D0 * (1.0 + 0.9 * np.exp(-((xx - 3.0) ** 2 + (yy - 1.0) ** 2) / 1.5))
    p_variable, _, _, _ = solve(potential, solid, diffusion_field, start, 120.0)
    prediction = steady_state(potential, solid, D0)

    open_cells = ~solid & (prediction > 1e-5)
    ratios = p_variable[open_cells] / prediction[open_cells]

    print("\nBarrier delays mixing:")
    for t in (2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0, 60.0):
        k = int(np.argmin(np.abs(record_times - t)))
        print(
            f"  t = {record_times[k]:5.1f} h"
            f"   TV to equilibrium: barrier {error_barrier[k]:.4f}"
            f"   no barrier {error_free[k]:.4f}"
        )

    max_rel_err = float(
        np.max(
            np.abs(
                p_free[open_cells] / p_free.sum() - equilibrium[open_cells] / equilibrium.sum()
            )
            / equilibrium[open_cells]
        )
    )

    corr = float(
        np.corrcoef(np.log(p_variable[open_cells]), -potential[open_cells] / D0)[0, 1]
    )

    print("\nSolver validation (constant D, no barrier):")
    print(f"  max relative error versus exp(-U/D): {max_rel_err:.4f}")
    print(f"  TV distance at t = 60 h:             {error_free[-1]:.5f}")

    print("\nVariable diffusion versus the constant-D Boltzmann prediction:")
    print(f"  median ratio p_steady / (exp(-U/D0) normalised): {np.median(ratios):.3f}")
    print(
        f"  interquartile range of ratio:                    "
        f"{np.subtract(*np.percentile(ratios, [75, 25])):.3f}"
    )
    print(f"  correlation of log p with -U/D0:                 {corr:.3f}")

    fig = _plot(
        xx,
        yy,
        potential,
        solid,
        equilibrium,
        record_times,
        error_barrier,
        error_free,
        open_cells,
        p_variable,
        diffusion_field,
    )

    output_path = Path(output)
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(output_path, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
    plt.close(fig)
    return output_path


def main() -> None:
    """Console-script entry point."""
    run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()



Habitat potential with the river and bridge (top left), the Boltzmann equilibrium for constant diffusion (top right), the total-variation relaxation with and without the river (bottom left), and the failure of the constant-diffusion Boltzmann law when diffusion varies (bottom right)


Three things are visible in the figure and confirmed by the printed diagnostics.
The equilibrium is bimodal. With two wells, \(e^{-U/D}\) has two humps. Defect 1 is repaired by construction: multi-modal utilization distributions are ordinary output, not something the modeler has to disbelieve.
The river slows mixing but does not change the equilibrium. No-flux walls cannot change a zero-current solution, so both landscapes relax towards the same \(p_\infty\); what the river changes is how long redistribution takes. Measured in total-variation distance to equilibrium:
Barrier delays mixing:
  t =   2.0 h   TV to equilibrium: barrier 0.4884   no barrier 0.3573
  t =   5.0 h   TV to equilibrium: barrier 0.4625   no barrier 0.2031
  t =  10.0 h   TV to equilibrium: barrier 0.4218   no barrier 0.0819
  t =  20.0 h   TV to equilibrium: barrier 0.3508   no barrier 0.0485
  t =  40.0 h   TV to equilibrium: barrier 0.2427   no barrier 0.0479
  t =  60.0 h   TV to equilibrium: barrier 0.1679   no barrier 0.0479
After sixty hours the free landscape has essentially settled while the riverine one is still far from it: the bridge is the only channel, and mixing is gated by its width. For management this is the difference between where animals will eventually be and where they can be reached in a season.
The solver has its own physics, again. With the river removed, the numerical steady state is compared against \(e^{-U/D}\) directly:
Solver validation (constant D, no barrier):
  max relative error versus exp(-U/D): 0.1683
  TV distance at t = 60 h:             0.04789
The error is not concentrated in the tails: the median relative error over open cells is about \(0.155\), because first-order upwinding of the drift adds an artificial diffusion of size roughly \(|b|\,\Delta x/2 \approx 0.06\ \text{km}^2/\text{h}\) against a physical \(D = 0.5\) — a twelve percent inflation of the effective diffusivity. Refining the grid from \(81^2\) to \(161^2\) halves both the median relative error (\(0.155 \to 0.078\)) and the total-variation distance (\(0.048 \to 0.024\)), the first-order convergence the scheme owes. This is the same lesson as in the OU post, now in two dimensions: solving the Fokker-Planck equation always means solving a discretization of it.
Finally, the variable-diffusion run. Where \(D\) varies, \(e^{-U/D_0}\) is no longer the stationary density:
Variable diffusion versus the constant-D Boltzmann prediction:
  median ratio p_steady / (exp(-U/D0) normalised): 1.461
  interquartile range of ratio:                    0.721
  correlation of log p with -U/D0:                 0.943
The potential still organizes the density — the correlation stays high — but no longer determines it: the equilibrium is shifted by almost fifty percent at the median, with a spread of the same order. There is no universal closed-form equilibrium left to check a solver against; where movement ease varies across a landscape, the pattern of \(D\) matters as much as the pattern of \(U\), and solving the PDE is not optional.

title: A General Fokker-Planck Model of Moose Movement
section: Experiment 2: three repairs in one dimension
text:
Experiment 2: three repairs in one dimension
The second script isolates three of the general mechanisms in one dimension, where each can be checked against something.
"""Three ways of repairing the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model of moose movement.

1. Fractional diffusion: replace the Laplacian by the fractional Laplacian of
   order 2 alpha, so the Fokker-Planck operator becomes
       dp/dt = -d/dx (b p) + D (-d^2/dx^2)^alpha p ,
   and the stationary density acquires power-law tails instead of decaying
   like a Gaussian. Solved with a split scheme: the exact Ornstein-Uhlenbeck
   contraction, remapped conservatively cell by cell, then exact fractional
   diffusion applied in Fourier space.

2. Nonlocal interaction: add a McKean-Vlasov drift that pulls each animal
   towards the local density of animals, in the form
       b(x) = -kappa x + chi d/dx log(G * p) .
   Solved with the explicit finite-volume scheme until it stops changing.

3. Behavioural states: two coupled Fokker-Planck equations for a moose that
   switches between a tight core range and a wider exploratory mode.
       dp_i/dt = -d/dx (b_i p_i) + D_i d^2p_i/dx^2 + q_ji p_j - q_ij p_i
   Solved in time from a point mass, then compared against a single-state
   Ornstein-Uhlenbeck fit.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter1d

from moose_fp.numerics import total_variation

ALPHA = 0.5  # Fractional order of the diffusion operator / 2
KAPPA = 1.0  # OU fidelity, 1/h
DIFFUSION = 1.0  # Diffusion coefficient, km^2/h


def flow_contract(p, x, a):
    """Push cell masses through the exact OU contraction x -> x/a.

    The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck drift -kappa x points inward everywhere, so the
    deterministic flow of one step maps the domain into itself without any
    wraparound: mass in the outer strips moves in and leaves a hole near the
    seam, which the diffusion step then refills. The remap reads mass off the
    cumulative distribution and conserves it exactly.
    """
    nodes = np.append(x, x[-1] + (x[1] - x[0]))
    cumulative = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(p)))
    preimages = np.clip(a * nodes, nodes[0], nodes[-1])
    moved = np.interp(preimages, nodes, cumulative)
    return moved[1:] - moved[:-1]


def fractional_ou(alpha, n_steps, dt, grid, length):
    """Stationary density of the fractional OU process on a periodic domain.

    Returns ``(x, p, spacing, mass_drift)`` where ``p`` is normalised as a
    density and ``mass_drift`` is the largest deviation from total mass one
    seen over the run.
    """
    x = -0.5 * length + np.arange(grid) * (length / grid)
    spacing = length / grid
    k = 2.0 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(grid, d=spacing)

    p = np.exp(-0.5 * KAPPA * x**2)
    p /= p.sum()

    contraction = np.exp(KAPPA * dt)
    evolved = np.exp(-DIFFUSION * np.abs(k) ** (2.0 * alpha) * dt)

    low = high = p.sum()
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        p = flow_contract(p, x, contraction)
        p = np.real(np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(p) * evolved))
        low = min(low, p.sum())
        high = max(high, p.sum())

    p = p / (p.sum() * spacing)
    return x, p, spacing, high - low


def advance_periodic(p, drift, spacing, diffusion, dt):
    """Conservative explicit step for dp/dt = -d/dx (b p) + d^2 (D p)/dx^2."""
    b_face = 0.5 * (drift + np.roll(drift, -1))
    upwind = np.where(b_face > 0.0, p, np.roll(p, -1))
    flux = upwind * b_face - diffusion * (np.roll(p, -1) - p) / spacing
    p = p - dt * (flux - np.roll(flux, 1)) / spacing
    return np.maximum(p, 0.0)


def drift_habitat(x):
    """The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck restoring drift -kappa x."""
    return -KAPPA * x


def interaction_run(chi, grid, length, dt, t_end, width, tolerance=1e-10):
    """Equilibrium with a nonlocal attraction towards the animal density.

    Returns ``(x, p, elapsed_time, final_change)``.
    """
    x = -0.5 * length + np.arange(grid) * (length / grid)
    spacing = length / grid

    p = np.exp(-0.5 * KAPPA * x**2)
    p /= p.sum()

    n_steps = round(t_end / dt)
    previous = p.copy()
    change = float("nan")
    for step in range(n_steps):
        drift = drift_habitat(x)
        if chi != 0.0:
            smoothed = gaussian_filter1d(p, sigma=width / spacing, mode="nearest")
            smoothed = np.maximum(smoothed, 1e-14 * smoothed.max())
            drift = drift + chi * np.gradient(np.log(smoothed), spacing)
        p = advance_periodic(p, drift, spacing, DIFFUSION, dt)
        if step % 200 == 0 and step > 0:
            change = 0.5 * np.sum(np.abs(p - previous))
            if change < tolerance:
                return x, p, (step + 1) * dt, change
            previous = p.copy()

    return x, p, n_steps * dt, change


def self_consistent_variance(chi, width, iterations=400):
    """Fixed point of v = D / (kappa + chi / (v + width^2)) for a Gaussian."""
    variance = DIFFUSION / KAPPA
    for _ in range(iterations):
        variance = DIFFUSION / (KAPPA + chi / (variance + width**2))
    return variance


def face_flux(p, drift, spacing, diffusion):
    """Advective (upwinded) plus diffusive flux on the cell faces."""
    flux = np.zeros(len(p) + 1)
    interior_b = 0.5 * (drift[:-1] + drift[1:])
    interior = (
        np.where(interior_b > 0.0, p[:-1], p[1:]) * interior_b
        - diffusion * (p[1:] - p[:-1]) / spacing
    )
    flux[1:-1] = interior
    return flux


def switch_run(x, spacing, dt, t_end, snapshot_at):
    """Time-dependent solution of the two coupled state equations.

    Returns a dict mapping each requested snapshot time to ``(p_a, p_b)``.
    """
    state_a = {"kappa": 1.0, "centre": -3.0, "diffusion": 0.25, "out": 0.10}
    state_b = {"kappa": 0.5, "centre": 2.5, "diffusion": 0.60, "out": 0.10}

    p_a = np.where(np.isclose(x, -3.0), 1.0, 0.0)
    p_b = np.zeros_like(p_a)
    p_a /= p_a.sum()

    n_steps = round(t_end / dt)
    snapshots = {}
    for step in range(n_steps):
        flux_a = face_flux(
            p_a, -state_a["kappa"] * (x - state_a["centre"]), spacing, state_a["diffusion"]
        )
        flux_b = face_flux(
            p_b, -state_b["kappa"] * (x - state_b["centre"]), spacing, state_b["diffusion"]
        )

        p_a_next = p_a - dt * (flux_a[1:] - flux_a[:-1]) / spacing
        p_b_next = p_b - dt * (flux_b[1:] - flux_b[:-1]) / spacing

        p_a_next += dt * (-state_a["out"] * p_a + state_b["out"] * p_b)
        p_b_next += dt * (-state_b["out"] * p_b + state_a["out"] * p_a)

        p_a = np.maximum(p_a_next, 0.0)
        p_b = np.maximum(p_b_next, 0.0)

        for when in snapshot_at:
            if abs((step + 1) * dt - when) < 0.5 * dt:
                snapshots[when] = (p_a.copy(), p_b.copy())

    return snapshots


def sample_path(grid_dt, t_end, seed=20261016):
    """One representative animal path with switching behaviour.

    Returns ``(times, position, states)``.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = round(t_end / grid_dt)
    times = np.arange(n + 1) * grid_dt

    states = np.zeros(n + 1, dtype=int)
    position = np.zeros(n + 1)
    for i in range(n):
        states[i + 1] = states[i]
        if rng.random() < 0.10 * grid_dt:
            states[i + 1] = 1 - states[i]

        current = states[i + 1]
        kappa, centre, diffusion = [
            (1.0, -3.0, 0.25),
            (0.5, 2.5, 0.60),
        ][current]
        drift = -kappa * (position[i] - centre)
        position[i + 1] = (
            position[i] + drift * grid_dt + np.sqrt(2.0 * diffusion * grid_dt) * rng.normal()
        )
    return times, position, states


def _plot(x_f, p_alpha1, p_alphahalf, gaussian, slope, intercept, x_i, p_free,
          p_inter, x_s, mixture, p_a, p_b, gaussian_fit, times, path):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    ax = axes[0, 0]
    core = (x_f > 0.4) & (x_f < 10.0) & (p_alpha1 > 1e-12)
    ax.loglog(x_f[core], p_alpha1[core], color="steelblue", linewidth=2,
              label=r"$\alpha = 1$ (Gaussian)")
    ax.loglog(x_f[core], gaussian[core], color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5,
              label="exact Gaussian")
    tail_alpha = (x_f > 0.4) & (x_f < 10.0) & (p_alphahalf > 1e-14)
    ax.loglog(x_f[tail_alpha], p_alphahalf[tail_alpha], color="darkred", linewidth=2,
              label=r"$\alpha = 0.5$")
    reference = np.exp(intercept) * (x_f[tail_alpha] ** slope)
    ax.loglog(x_f[tail_alpha], reference, color="darkorange", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5,
              label=f"tail slope {slope:.2f}")
    ax.set_xlabel("distance from home range centre (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("stationary density")
    ax.set_title("Fractional diffusion gives power-law tails")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    ax = axes[0, 1]
    ax.plot(x_i, p_free, color="steelblue", linewidth=2,
            label=r"$\chi = 0$ (independent moose)")
    ax.plot(x_i, p_inter, color="darkred", linewidth=2,
            label=r"$\chi = 0.6$ (nonlocal attraction)")
    ax.set_xlabel("distance from home range centre (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("stationary density")
    ax.set_title("Interaction makes the herd bunch together")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    ax = axes[1, 0]
    ax.fill_between(x_s, mixture, color="grey", alpha=0.35, label="total density")
    ax.plot(x_s, p_a, color="steelblue", linewidth=2, label="state A: core range")
    ax.plot(x_s, p_b, color="darkred", linewidth=2, label="state B: exploratory")
    ax.plot(x_s, gaussian_fit, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5,
            label="single-state fit")
    ax.set_xlabel("distance from home range centre (km)")
    ax.set_ylabel("stationary density")
    ax.set_title("Behavioural states turn one Gaussian into two lobes")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    ax = axes[1, 1]
    for _mode, colour, label in ((0, "steelblue", "state A"), (1, "darkred", "state B")):
        ax.scatter(times, path, s=2.5, color=colour, label=label, rasterized=True)
    ax.set_xlabel("t (h)")
    ax.set_ylabel("position (km)")
    ax.set_title("One animal switching between behaviours")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9, markerscale=3)

    fig.suptitle("Beyond the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model")
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig


def run(output: str | Path = "figures/beyond_gaussian_fp.png") -> Path:
    """Run the three one-dimensional repairs, print diagnostics, write figure."""
    # --- Fractional tails ------------------------------------------------
    x_f, p_alpha1, spacing_f, _mass_alpha1 = fractional_ou(
        alpha=1.0, n_steps=20000, dt=0.005, grid=2048, length=32.0
    )
    x_f, p_alphahalf, _, _mass_alphahalf = fractional_ou(
        alpha=ALPHA, n_steps=20000, dt=0.005, grid=2048, length=32.0
    )

    gaussian = KAPPA * np.exp(-0.5 * KAPPA * x_f**2) / np.sqrt(2.0 * np.pi * DIFFUSION)
    tv_alpha1 = total_variation(p_alpha1, gaussian, spacing_f)

    tail = (x_f > 2.5) & (x_f < 6.0) & (p_alphahalf > 1e-14)
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log(x_f[tail]), np.log(p_alphahalf[tail]), 1)

    print("Fractional OU, 20000 split steps of 0.005 h, 2048 points on [-16, 16) km")
    print(f"  alpha = 1:   mass drift over the run {_mass_alpha1:.3e}")
    print(f"  alpha = 0.5: mass drift over the run {_mass_alphahalf:.3e}")
    print(f"  alpha = 1 TV distance to the exact Gaussian: {tv_alpha1:.4f}")
    print(f"  alpha = 0.5 tail fit on 2.5-6 km: slope {slope:.3f} (predicted -2.000)")

    # --- Nonlocal interaction -------------------------------------------
    width = 0.5
    interaction_grid = 256
    interaction_spacing = 16.0 / interaction_grid
    dt = 0.2 * interaction_spacing**2 / DIFFUSION
    x_i, p_free, t_free, change_free = interaction_run(
        0.0, interaction_grid, 16.0, dt, 400.0, width
    )
    x_i, p_inter, t_inter, change_inter = interaction_run(
        0.6, interaction_grid, 16.0, dt, 400.0, width
    )

    def variance(p):
        mean = float(np.sum(p * x_i))
        return float(np.sum(p * x_i**2)) - mean**2

    v_free, v_inter = variance(p_free), variance(p_inter)
    v_predicted = self_consistent_variance(0.6, width)
    gaussian_predicted = np.exp(-0.5 * x_i**2 / v_predicted)
    gaussian_predicted /= gaussian_predicted.sum()
    tv_prediction = total_variation(p_inter, gaussian_predicted)
    tv_equilibria = total_variation(p_inter, p_free)

    print(f"\nNonlocal attraction chi = 0.6 km^2/h, interaction width {width} km")
    print(f"  converged after {t_free:.1f} h (chi = 0) and {t_inter:.1f} h (chi = 0.6)")
    print(f"  final TV change: {change_free:.2e} and {change_inter:.2e}")
    print(f"  variance: no interaction {v_free:.3f}, with interaction {v_inter:.3f}")
    print(f"  self-consistent Gaussian prediction: {v_predicted:.3f}")
    print(f"  TV distance from that prediction: {tv_prediction:.3f}")
    print(f"  TV distance between the two equilibria: {tv_equilibria:.3f}")

    # --- Behavioural states ----------------------------------------------
    grid_s, length_s = 384, 16.0
    spacing_s = length_s / grid_s
    x_s = -0.5 * length_s + np.arange(grid_s) * spacing_s
    dt_s = 0.25 * spacing_s**2 / 0.60

    snapshots = switch_run(x_s, spacing_s, dt_s, 100.0, snapshot_at=(60.0, 100.0))
    p_a, p_b = snapshots[100.0]
    mixture = p_a + p_b

    mean = float(np.sum(mixture * x_s))
    sd = float(np.sqrt(np.sum(mixture * (x_s - mean) ** 2)))
    gaussian_fit = np.exp(-0.5 * ((x_s - mean) / sd) ** 2)
    gaussian_fit /= gaussian_fit.sum()

    tv_gaussian = total_variation(mixture, gaussian_fit)
    tv_stationary = total_variation(
        snapshots[60.0][0] + snapshots[60.0][1], mixture
    )
    midpoint_ratio = float(mixture[np.isclose(x_s, 0.0)][0]) / float(np.max(mixture))

    print("\nTwo behavioural states, 100 h of switching (10 h typical per state)")
    print(f"  mass in state A {np.sum(p_a):.6f}, state B {np.sum(p_b):.6f}")
    print(f"  change between t = 60 h and t = 100 h: TV {tv_stationary:.2e}")
    print(f"  mixture mean {mean:.3f} km, sd {sd:.3f} km")
    print(f"  TV distance from a single Gaussian with the same mean and sd: {tv_gaussian:.3f}")
    print(f"  density at the midpoint versus the highest mode: {midpoint_ratio:.3f}")

    times, path, _states = sample_path(0.005, 100.0)
    fraction_wide = float(np.mean(_states == 1))
    print(f"  example path: {fraction_wide:.3f} of the time in the wide mode")

    # --- Figure ----------------------------------------------------------
    fig = _plot(
        x_f,
        p_alpha1,
        p_alphahalf,
        gaussian,
        slope,
        intercept,
        x_i,
        p_free,
        p_inter,
        x_s,
        mixture,
        p_a,
        p_b,
        gaussian_fit,
        times,
        path,
    )

    output_path = Path(output)
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(output_path, dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
    plt.close(fig)
    return output_path


def main() -> None:
    """Console-script entry point."""
    run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()



Power-law tails from fractional diffusion (top left), bunching under nonlocal attraction (top right), the two behavioural states and their single-state fit (bottom left), and one animal switching between them (bottom right)


Fractional diffusion gives the moose heavy tails. The stationary density of the fractional OU flow is computed by a split scheme: each step applies the exact Ornstein-Uhlenbeck contraction, remapped conservatively from cell to cell, and then the exact fractional diffusion in Fourier space. As a check, \(\alpha = 1\) must reproduce the ordinary Gaussian, and does, to a total-variation distance of \(0.0037\) over twenty thousand steps with mass drift at the \(10^{-12}\) level. For \(\alpha = 0.5\) the stationary density is no longer Gaussian in the tails:
Fractional OU, 20000 split steps of 0.005 h, 2048 points on [-16, 16) km
  alpha = 1:   mass drift over the run 9.237e-12
  alpha = 0.5: mass drift over the run 2.734e-12
  alpha = 1 TV distance to the exact Gaussian: 0.0037
  alpha = 0.5 tail fit on 2.5-6 km: slope -1.985 (predicted -2.000)
A fitted tail slope of \(-1.985\) against the predicted \(-(1+2\alpha) = -2\): the fractional moose still concentrates near its centre, but its rare multi-kilometre relocations occur at a power-law rate rather than the astronomical improbability the Gaussian assigns them. The numerical point worth keeping is that the flow step must be conservative. On the periodic domain used here the OU contraction points strictly inward, so the exact one-step map folds nothing across the seam; treating it as a wrap-around contraction would manufacture mass on every step, and the scheme would explode.
Nonlocal attraction makes the herd bunch together. With the interaction drift \(\chi \, \partial_x \log(G*p)\), the equilibrium can still be predicted: for a Gaussian \(p\) of variance \(v\), the smoothed density \(G*p\) is Gaussian of variance \(v + w^2\), so \(\log(G*p)\) is exactly quadratic and the self-consistency condition closes,
\[v = \frac{D}{\kappa + \chi/(v + w^2)}.\]
For \(\chi = 0.6\ \text{km}^2/\text{h}\) and interaction width \(w = 0.5\) km its fixed point is \(v = 0.581\), down from the non-interacting value of \(1\). The simulation:
Nonlocal attraction chi = 0.6 km^2/h, interaction width 0.5 km
  converged after 9.1 h (chi = 0) and 8.8 h (chi = 0.6)
  final TV change: 8.31e-11 and 7.78e-11
  variance: no interaction 1.050, with interaction 0.632
  self-consistent Gaussian prediction: 0.581
  TV distance from that prediction: 0.018
  TV distance between the two equilibria: 0.122
The interacting equilibrium sits within \(0.018\) of the predicted Gaussian; the residual, and the gap between \(0.632\) and \(0.581\), come from the same upwind numerical diffusion that inflated the free variance to \(1.050\) in the first place. The two equilibria are \(0.122\) apart in total variation: animals that pay attention to each other occupy a visibly tighter range than the same animals alone.
Behavioural states turn one Gaussian into two lobes. The last experiment couples two state equations: state A is a core range (\(\kappa = 1\ \text{h}^{-1}\), \(D = 0.25\ \text{km}^2/\text{h}\), centre \(-3\) km), state B an exploratory mode (\(\kappa = 0.5\ \text{h}^{-1}\), \(D = 0.6\ \text{km}^2/\text{h}\), centre \(+2.5\) km), with symmetric switching at \(0.1\ \text{h}^{-1}\) — a typical ten hours per state:
Two behavioural states, 100 h of switching (10 h typical per state)
  mass in state A 0.500000, state B 0.500000
  change between t = 60 h and t = 100 h: TV 4.14e-06
  mixture mean -0.462 km, sd 2.553 km
  TV distance from a single Gaussian with the same mean and sd: 0.340
  density at the midpoint versus the highest mode: 0.184
  example path: 0.261 of the time in the wide mode
By \(t = 60\) h the mixture is stationary. Its total density has two lobes with a dip at the midpoint to \(0.184\) of the peak height, and it is \(0.340\) away from the best single Gaussian with the same mean and variance — far beyond any discretization error. This is the quantitative form of the argument that made switching state-space models standard in movement ecology (Jonsen et al. 2007; Patterson et al. 2009): a single-state model fitted to such an animal invents a home range centred in the gap between the two lobes, habitat the moose in fact avoids.

title: A General Fokker-Planck Model of Moose Movement
text:
What generality does not buy
Repairs have prices, and honesty requires listing them.

None of this is fitted. Every parameter above was chosen to make the mechanism legible. The OU model at least admitted likelihood fitting through its Kalman filter; the general equation loses the linear-Gaussian structure that made that cheap (Hooten et al. 2017). Model inference, not model construction, is now the bottleneck.
Identifiability is the next wall. The equilibrium is shaped jointly by \(U\) and \(D\), and from positions alone good habitat is hard to distinguish from easy movement. Multi-lobed densities are produced by multi-modal potentials, by behavioural switching, by heavy tails, and by interactions alike; distinguishing mechanisms will need transients or multi-animal data, not just stationary utilizations.
Infinite speed is not repaired, only reinterpreted. Fractional diffusion replaces Gaussian steps with explicit jumps, but the operator is nonlocal in space, so influence still propagates instantly. The hard maximum-speed bounds from the first post live outside any Fokker-Planck model and remain complementary to it.
It is still a stationary framework. Season, snow, and rut enter here only through the choice of behavioural states, not as explicit time-dependence; defect 7 is partially, not fully, answered.
It costs compute. Two-dimensional grids, nonlocal couplings, and fractional operators turn closed forms into matrix and FFT work. Minutes on a laptop for the toy domains here; realistic landscapes demand more.

title: A General Fokker-Planck Model of Moose Movement
text:
Conclusion
The defect list from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck post served as a specification, and term by term the general Fokker-Planck equation carries what the OU model could not: a habitat potential that makes the home range multi-modal, a diffusion field that makes terrain matter, barriers that gate mixing through single crossings, conspecific attraction that tightens ranges, behavioural states that split one utilization distribution into two, and fractional diffusion that gives rare relocations a power-law rate. The OU model is not discarded — it survives as the special case these terms are switched off into, and as the null model every term is measured against. What is given up is everything that made the OU model computable: the Gaussian, the closed form, the filter. The next serious step is turning from model construction to model fitting, putting real collar fixes on the likelihood of some chosen subset of these terms.

title: A Generalization of Subindependence
text:
I was contemplating the notion of subindependence. It states that for two random variables on a shared probability space that the characteristic function of their sum is equal to the scalar product of their individual characteristic functions:
\[\phi_{X+Y} = \phi_{X}(t) \phi_{Y}(t).\]

title: A Generalization of Subindependence
text:
I was contemplating the notion of subindependence. It states that for two random variables on a shared probability space that the characteristic function of their sum is equal to the scalar product of their individual characteristic functions:
\[\phi_{X+Y} = \phi_{X}(t) \phi_{Y}(t).\]

title: A Generalization of Subindependence
text:
Multiple Variables
The first obvious generalization of this definition is to go to a collection of random variables \(\{X_1, \ldots, X_n \}\):
\[\phi_{\{X_1 + X_2 + \cdots +  X_n \}}(t) = \prod_{j=1}^n \phi_{X_{j}}(t)\]

title: A Generalization of Subindependence
text:
Choice of Operator
Instead of just considering the sum of random variables, we could generalize to a measurable function \(\odot: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \mapsto \mathcal{Z}\).
\[\phi_{\{X_1 \odot X_2 \odot \cdots \odot X_n \}}(t) = \prod_{j=1}^n \phi_{X_{j}}(t).\]
This has a familiarity to it. Like how Fourier transforms are related to sums of independent random variables or Mellin transforms under certain assumptions are related to products of independent random variables. I have not thought about this enough lately, but perhaps one can formalize this as a class of diagonalization decompositions in a function space.

title: A Generalization of Subindependence
text:
Copula Theory
Also, I wonder how subindependence relates to copula theory. Sklar’s theorem gives us general conditions for mapping the marginal probabilities to their joint probabilities via a copula. So in a sense copulae specify how collections of random variables are dependent (or independent, in the case of the independence copula). Anyway, I intuit that there is a connection here.

title: A Generalization of Subindependence
text:
Conclusions
Just sharing passerby impressions of the notion of independence. It seems like something that can readily be generalized, although I did not cover any mathematical or practical application.

title: Hacking The Data To Meet The Assumptions
text:
Introduction
This post is an ongoing series of posts that respond to the following video:


There is a particular quote from near the end of the video that I would like to explore. Dustin says this about rank-based procedures:

Quotation (Dustin Fife)
You’re hacking the data to meet the assumptions.

A natural question for me to start with is: what assumptions?
I think for a lot of people that take a statistics course they are given a collection of pre-made recipes to master. A typical frequentist course on statistics often covers an assortment of null hypothesis significance testing procedures that make particular assumptions. I already commented to an extent on the non-necessity of these procedures and assumptions for parametric statistics in Wilcoxon’s Heuristic.
I’ve seen some people try really hard to conform their analysis to such recipes. This often comes in the form of applying functions (AKA transformations) to obtain estimates that are unbiased, consistent, sufficient, or efficient, or similarly satisfying the Gauss-Markov theorem.
Often, although not always or not to the same extent, this comes from people not having the tools and knowledge to develop their own statistical methodologies. This is in part due to not having sufficient familiarity with mathematics or computer science. I expect that we’re all doing this to an extent; taking the approaches we have in hand conforming the problem to the tools. I am reminded of this quote which is purportedly from Amos Tversky:

Quotation (Amos Tversky)
Whenever there is a simple error that most laymen fall for, there is always a slightly more sophisticated version of the same problem that experts fall for.

But I wouldn’t say that all this adjusting to meet assumptions is entirely bad, especially if it is done rigorously. It is a matter of satisfying the goals and constraints of the analysis given the tools and the data in hand.
Functions, especially invertible functions, provide a means of making a hard problem easy. Physicists routinely apply what they call change of coordinates, which are just invertible functions, if it makes the problem they are working on easier. While there are complicated or sophisticated approaches involving integral transforms that are often used, I think there is a relatively simple example that we can draw on for intuition: polar coordinates. Often our data is supposed to be embedded in Cartesian coordinates, but sometimes the mathematics (and ‘shape of our data’ so-to-speak) becomes simpler if we convert to polar coordinates. If our data is a sample from a manifold which is a circle in Cartesian coordinates, then our data just becomes a line in polar coordinates. Likewise, many complicated curves on the plane just become polynomials or other tractable examples in polar coordinates.






Tip



Invertible functions are nice, but sometimes we have to do without them, or generalize what we mean by “inverse”. One approach that I’ve seen in Copula Theory is to take the infimum of the preimage of the function. With inverting matrices, which represent linear maps, we have the Moore-Penrose inverse. Or sometimes functions are not invertible but they are locally invertible via the inverse function theorem (IVT). And even when IVT fails because we don’t have partial derivatives we can turn to weak derivatives and distributional derivatives to obtain a similar relaxation of the Jacobians. See Tao 2009 for further reference on the distributional approach.


As (I think) I’ve mentioned before, the best use cases for rank-based statistics (Wilcoxon 1945) pertain to certain problems where the order properties of the data are of interest. While many people have used Wilcoxon’s heuristic as I’ve described it, I don’t think of them as synonymous with that approach. By all means use the Mann-Whitney U statistic (Mann and Whitney 1947) if you want to quantify the strength of a stochastic ordering between two groups as the statistic itself doesn’t assume very much at all. You can even compute the statistic on non-numerical data provided that the notion of order relation (i.e. what we mean by “\(\leq\)”) is defined. You can use the classic Mann-Whitney U test if

you can assign a non-arbitrary significance level threshold \(\alpha\) and
can assume the observations are soundly modelled as IID random variables and
you are actually interested in what it would say about the order properties of your data.

Otherwise, don’t use it. 🤷
There’s no shortage of mathematical modifications you can make to existing procedures if they don’t quite match what you’re going for. If a Mann-Whitney U test is almost what you want except that you cannot assume IID, then further develop a modification of the procedure that accounts for the statistical dependence. Maybe you further assume that the observations have a multivariate normal distribution, for example. Likewise, you can get out a dry eraser and whiteboard and start working out a new procedure from first principles.
Overall my impression of “you’re hacking the data to meet the assumptions” is that this isn’t necessarily as bad as it sounds. Sure, some people are producing janky work because they’re desperately trying to make something work that doesn’t work. However I think that Dustin may be thinking he is separating the wheat from the chaff when he is actually throwing out the baby with the bathwater… Figures of speech are weird. 🤔
Anyway, my point being that provided that it is done rigorously I do not think that rank-based non-parametric statistics (including the classics) are problematic per se. Where Dustin and I may find some agreement is that they often are not applied rigorously by people.
In my view we should challenge specific misuses of statistics when they arise rather than calling for an overly-broad abolition of what is basically a branch of math.





References

Mann, Henry B., and Donald R. Whitney. 1947. “On a Test of Whether One of Two Random Variables Is Stochastically Larger Than the Other.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 18 (1): 50–60. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177730491.


Wilcoxon, Frank. 1945. “Individual Comparisons by Ranking Methods.” Biometrics Bulletin 1 (6): 80–83. https://doi.org/10.2307/3001968.

title: Indivisible Stochastic Processes and the Stochastic–Quantum Correspondence
text:
The standard formulation of quantum theory rests on the Dirac–von Neumann axioms: states are vectors (or density matrices) in a Hilbert space, observables are self-adjoint operators, isolated systems evolve by a unitary operator (equivalently, by the Schrödinger equation), and measurement outcomes are governed by the Born rule (Dirac 1930; Neumann 1932). These axioms are empirically magnificent but conceptually divided: they treat “measurement” as an unexplained primitive and offer no account of what is happening in an experiment before a measurement is complete.
In a series of recent papers, Jacob Barandes has argued that a quantum system can instead be understood as a perfectly ordinary stochastic process unfolding in an old-fashioned configuration space, governed by probabilistic laws that are non-Markovian in a specific and previously unstudied sense. The central object is the indivisible stochastic process, and the central result is the stochastic–quantum correspondence (Barandes 2025b, 2025a):

Indivisible stochastic processes generically exhibit all the hallmark empirical features of quantum systems, including interference, decoherence, entanglement, and noncommutative observables, and a quantum system evolving unitarily can be understood as an indivisible stochastic process in disguise.

The payoff is a reformulation in which the Hilbert space and its ingredients—wave functions, state vectors, and Hamiltonians—are derived mathematical appurtenances rather than axioms, and in which the “measurement problem” is dissolved rather than solved.
The purpose of this post is to give a compact but self-contained account of the correspondence. I assume familiarity with probability and statistics, linear algebra, and the basics of quantum mechanics. Part I collects only the definitions the argument uses explicitly — stochastic processes, transition probabilities, Markovianity, divisibility, and stochastic matrices on the one hand; Hilbert spaces, states, observables, quantum channels, and unistochastic matrices on the other — and everything else is treated as known. I then give the formal definition of an indivisible stochastic process, the precise sense in which it fails to be Markovian, the dictionary that connects it to a Hilbert space, the Kraus and Stinespring machinery that yields unitary evolution, and finally the stochastic–quantum theorem itself. Throughout, definitions, lemmas, propositions, and theorems are stated formally and, where instructive, proved.

title: Indivisible Stochastic Processes and the Stochastic–Quantum Correspondence
text:
The standard formulation of quantum theory rests on the Dirac–von Neumann axioms: states are vectors (or density matrices) in a Hilbert space, observables are self-adjoint operators, isolated systems evolve by a unitary operator (equivalently, by the Schrödinger equation), and measurement outcomes are governed by the Born rule (Dirac 1930; Neumann 1932). These axioms are empirically magnificent but conceptually divided: they treat “measurement” as an unexplained primitive and offer no account of what is happening in an experiment before a measurement is complete.
In a series of recent papers, Jacob Barandes has argued that a quantum system can instead be understood as a perfectly ordinary stochastic process unfolding in an old-fashioned configuration space, governed by probabilistic laws that are non-Markovian in a specific and previously unstudied sense. The central object is the indivisible stochastic process, and the central result is the stochastic–quantum correspondence (Barandes 2025b, 2025a):

Indivisible stochastic processes generically exhibit all the hallmark empirical features of quantum systems, including interference, decoherence, entanglement, and noncommutative observables, and a quantum system evolving unitarily can be understood as an indivisible stochastic process in disguise.

The payoff is a reformulation in which the Hilbert space and its ingredients—wave functions, state vectors, and Hamiltonians—are derived mathematical appurtenances rather than axioms, and in which the “measurement problem” is dissolved rather than solved.
The purpose of this post is to give a compact but self-contained account of the correspondence. I assume familiarity with probability and statistics, linear algebra, and the basics of quantum mechanics. Part I collects only the definitions the argument uses explicitly — stochastic processes, transition probabilities, Markovianity, divisibility, and stochastic matrices on the one hand; Hilbert spaces, states, observables, quantum channels, and unistochastic matrices on the other — and everything else is treated as known. I then give the formal definition of an indivisible stochastic process, the precise sense in which it fails to be Markovian, the dictionary that connects it to a Hilbert space, the Kraus and Stinespring machinery that yields unitary evolution, and finally the stochastic–quantum theorem itself. Throughout, definitions, lemmas, propositions, and theorems are stated formally and, where instructive, proved.
A reader who wants the conceptual through-line rather than the full machinery may read the introduction to each part and the statements of the main results, and treat the proofs and technical definitions as a reference.
